cards.explanation: The answer is that the priest pronounces the person unclean. He sees two things at once: the hair in the spot has turned white, and the sore appears deeper than the skin. Leviticus 13:3 says, “…it is a skin disease. After the priest examines him, he must pronounce him unclean.” I don't pull a batch out of the oven on a hunch either. I look first, and so does the priest.

The answer is seven. Leviticus 13:4 says the priest “…shall isolate the infected person for seven days.” That's the in-between answer for a spot that isn't clearly a disease yet. It's a week of letting the spot show what it really is.

The answer is False. The person is not clean yet. Leviticus 13:5 says that if the infection is unchanged and hasn't spread, “…the priest must isolate him for another seven days.” A second week, then the priest examines again (Leviticus 13:6). The ruling comes after that.

The answer is clean. Leviticus 13:6 says that if the sore has faded and hasn't spread, “…the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash.” The person must also wash his clothes and be clean. That's where the two weeks of waiting end.
The answer is clothes. Leviticus 13:6 says, “The person must wash his clothes and be clean.” It's a laundry day with good news attached, friends. I'd gladly do that wash.

The answer is a skin disease. Leviticus 13:8 says, “…the priest must pronounce him unclean; it is a skin disease.” The spread is what changes the answer, because the rash was clean after the first two weeks only while it stayed put. Once it moves, the verdict moves with it.

The answer is True. Leviticus 13:11 says, “…it is a chronic skin disease and the priest must pronounce him unclean.” Then it adds, “He need not isolate him, for he is unclean.” No maybe week here. When the signs are this plain, the priest says so right away.

The answer is that the person is clean. This one makes everybody do a double take, me too. Leviticus 13:13 says, “Since it has all turned white, he is clean.” The disease covering the whole body, all turned white, is what makes the priest pronounce clean. Then verse 14 adds that raw flesh makes someone unclean.

The answer is that the person is clean. Leviticus 13:17 says, “…if the infection has turned white, the priest is to pronounce the infected person clean; then he is clean.” White is the same word that made the head-to-foot case clean. The raw flesh was unclean (Leviticus 13:15), but once it turns white, the answer changes.

The answer is white hair and beneath the skin. Leviticus 13:20 says, “…if it appears to be beneath the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest shall pronounce him unclean…” Those are the same two signs we saw at the very start of the chapter. The priest is looking for the same pair.

The answer is scar. Leviticus 13:23 says, “…it is only the scar from the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.” A spot that stays the same and doesn't spread is only left over from the boil. It's a reminder, not a problem.

The answer is yellow and thin. Leviticus 13:30 says, “…if it appears to be deeper than the skin and the hair in it is yellow and thin, the priest must pronounce him unclean…” The text calls it “…a scaly outbreak…” Every spot has its own sign, and this one is hair that's yellow and thin.

The answer is to shave except for the scaly area. Leviticus 13:33 says, “…the person must shave himself except for the scaly area.” Then the priest isolates him for another seven days. On the seventh day, the priest examines the scaly outbreak again (Leviticus 13:34).

The answer is False. Leviticus 13:36 says that if the outbreak has spread, “…the priest need not look for yellow hair; the person is unclean.” The yellow hair mattered earlier, but once the outbreak spreads, there's no need to look. Spreading settles it.

The answer is that it has healed. Leviticus 13:37 says that if the outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, “…then it has healed. He is clean…” Black hair is the good sign here. Yellow hair meant trouble, so black hair is the opposite.

The answer is harmless, and it's good news. Leviticus 13:39 says, “…if the spots are dull white, it is a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin; the person is clean.” The priest looks, the spots are dull white, and the person is clean. I do a happy dance right here on my gold base. Dull white spots, harmless rash, clean.

The answer is False. Leviticus 13:40 says, “Now if a man loses his hair and is bald, he is still clean.” Verse 41 says a receding hairline is the same. The trouble comes only if there's a reddish-white sore on the bald head or forehead (Leviticus 13:42).

The answer is their mouth. Leviticus 13:45 says the person “…must cover his mouth and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean!’” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's a hard way to live, and it's good to read it plainly.

The answer is alone outside the camp. Leviticus 13:46 says, “As long as he has the infection, he remains unclean. He must live alone in a place outside the camp.” That is the place the text gives for a person who has the infection. I think this one hurts to read.

The answer is green and red. Leviticus 13:49 says, “…if the mark in the fabric, leather, weave, knit, or leather article is green or red, then it is contaminated with mildew and must be shown to the priest.” So a green mark means a trip to the priest, and so does a red one. Green and red together are the pair. Neither one gets a pass.

The answer is to isolate it for seven days. Leviticus 13:50 says, “…the priest is to examine the mildew and isolate the contaminated fabric for seven days.” That's the same as the maybe cases on the skin. The item gets its own seven-day wait.

The answer is that it is burned up. Leviticus 13:52 says, “Since the mildew is harmful, the article must be burned up.” That covers wool, linen or leather. Once the mildew has spread, the item is done.

The answer is False. Leviticus 13:55 says, “Even though the mildew has not spread, you must burn it, whether the rot is on the front or back.” The washing didn't change how it looks, so the item is unclean. Not spreading isn't enough here.

The answer is burn the item, friends! Leviticus 13:57 says, “But if it reappears in the fabric, weave, or knit, or on any leather article, it is spreading. You must burn the contaminated article.” The priest already tried cutting out the mildewed section in verse 56. When the mildew comes back, the text doesn't send him for a second snip. It says burn.

The answer is True. Leviticus 13:58 says, “If the mildew disappears from the fabric, weave, or knit, or any leather article after washing, then it is to be washed again, and it will be clean.” One more wash and the item is clean. A happy ending for a piece of laundry.
